slides.title: Geometry Without Continuity
slides.notes: Open by framing the appendix as a stress test for the entire course. Students have seen models of Euclidean, hyperbolic, and elliptic geometry; now the question is which parts of those stories used continuity without saying so. The title visual contrasts a finite laboratory with a projective completion because both are useful, but they license different kinds of inference.

slides.title: What survives after continuity is removed?
slides.notes: This slide should slow the room before the technical material begins. The point is not that continuity is wrong or dispensable everywhere. The point is that continuity is a separate permission. When it is absent, a proof must make do with incidence, perpendicularity, and transformations, or rebuild the missing analytic objects from algebra.

slides.title: H-Planes are the continuity-free starting point
slides.notes: Use this slide to separate vocabulary before the construction begins. H-plane language keeps the Hilbert style base visible, while absolute plane language highlights perpendicularity and reflection. Students should hear that the appendix is not abandoning rigor. It is changing the inventory of permitted objects and asking what can still be reconstructed.

slides.title: A four-step program replaces limits with structure
slides.notes: Present the program as the backbone of the appendix. Instead of assuming real coordinates at the beginning, the construction earns coordinates by projective completion. Instead of measuring perpendicularity with a metric already known to be real valued, it encodes perpendicularity algebraically. The payoff is a classification problem that can be stated in field language.

slides.title: New points are pencils of old lines
slides.notes: This is the first genuinely projective move. Old points are easy because the lines through the point already form a pencil. The second kind is controlled by perpendicularity to a fixed line. The third kind is the subtle one, because calling it an ideal point cannot depend on limiting parallel rays whose existence is under investigation.

slides.title: Parallel pencils are certified by reflections
slides.notes: Explain the formula as a definition by behavior. A line belongs to the third-kind pencil when the three reflected operations collapse back to a reflection. The audience does not need the full proof here. They need the logical discipline: the direction is detected by transformations available in the absolute plane, not by a completed boundary already assumed.

slides.title: One common line is pinned down by a reflection equation
slides.notes: Do not treat this as a copied figure; treat it as a schematic of the proof idea. The old point D supplies one pencil, and the parallel-direction pencil supplies the other. The constructed line b is not guessed from a drawing. It is forced by a reflection equation, which is exactly the kind of replacement for continuity the appendix is teaching.

slides.title: Old lines extend, but new lines are also needed
slides.notes: Point out that simply extending every old line is not enough for a full projective plane. The construction also needs lines made from poles and other completed incidence classes. The disk picture is only a model cue. The real definition is combinatorial and transformation based: which pencils are incident with which completed lines.

slides.title: Half-rotations manufacture projective lines
slides.notes: Use the diagram as an operational picture, not as a Euclidean proof. The reflection product around O behaves like a rotation, and the half-rotation sends A to a midpoint A*. The important feature is projective: these maps can carry completed lines to other completed lines, which helps verify the incidence axioms of the enlarged plane.

slides.title: Pappus supplies the field machinery
slides.notes: The Pappus slide is where the audience should see the algebra enter cleanly. Once the completed geometry has a projective and affine interpretation, a field of coordinates is no longer an imported real-number background. It is recovered from incidence. Stress that this is why continuity-free geometry can still become computationally precise.

slides.title: Betweenness defines positive scalars
slides.notes: This slide connects synthetic betweenness to algebraic order. The definition of positive scalar is not a measurement with a real ruler. It comes from ratios along a completed affine line and from invariance under parallel projection. Mention that a Menelaus-type theorem supplies the algebraic consistency needed for an ordered field.

slides.title: The field may be Pythagorean without being Euclidean
slides.notes: This is a good place to prevent a common misunderstanding. The coordinate field is not automatically the real numbers. Free mobility gives strong algebraic information, but elementary continuity adds a different strength: square roots for positive elements. That is why unusual non-Archimedean or non-Euclidean fields can support geometries that look familiar locally and strange globally.

slides.title: A single parameter controls orthogonality
slides.notes: The formula is the key algebraic compression of perpendicularity. It extends the relation to projective lines, assigns poles, and makes isotropic behavior visible. The parameter k is not decoration. Its sign and square-class behavior sort the geometry into different regimes, including cases with an empty absolute or self-perpendicular lines.

slides.title: The boundary appears from poles of isotropic lines
slides.notes: Use the equation to connect the previous slide to a geometric model. The absolute is the locus associated with isotropic behavior and poles. When k is negative the circle model is natural; when k is zero the Euclidean case emerges differently; when k is positive the real ordered picture has no ordinary circular absolute. The field still matters.

slides.title: Lambert quadrilaterals read the sign of k
slides.notes: Students have seen Lambert quadrilaterals earlier, so this slide reconnects the appendix with the course narrative. The fourth angle is acute, right, or obtuse according to the sign of k. That familiar geometric trichotomy is now explained by an algebraic parameter rather than by an assumed model of the real plane.

slides.title: Non-Archimedean fields create unfamiliar planes
slides.notes: Treat the table as a map, not as a list to memorize. The crucial idea is that changing the field or restricting the point domain changes the geometry while preserving enough synthetic structure to be an H-plane. On Archimedean fields the landscape is much narrower, but non-Archimedean fields reveal why continuity mattered.

slides.title: A finite model exposes missing limits
slides.notes: This slide connects the lecture deck to the assigned notebook. The finite grid is deliberately modest: it makes absence visible and forces students to distinguish construction from inference. It does not claim to classify H-planes. It prepares the mindset needed for the appendix, where missing continuity is handled by projective completion and algebra.

slides.title: Continuity-free geometry is still highly structured
slides.notes: Close by returning to the initial question. Geometry without continuity is not vague or merely finite; it is a disciplined reconstruction of structure from weaker assumptions. The appendix shows how projective incidence, reflections, Pappus coordinates, ordered fields, and a quadratic parameter can replace many hidden analytic habits while also revealing exactly where continuity changes the answer.
